cases.law_scope: Delhi, India — Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act, 1952, s.13(1) proviso (b)(i) and (c)(i), including the distinct consent requirements for post-Act and pre-Act sub-letting.
cases.target_stage: Supreme Court civil appeal (Civil Appeal No. 1249 of 1967) from the Delhi High Court judgment in Regular First Appeal No. 166-D of 1965.
cases.substantive_issue: Whether the appellant's grants of hotel rooms constituted sub-letting (tenant/sub-lessee rather than licensee occupation) and lacked the consent required under the applicable pre-/post-commencement limbs of s.13(1).

issue_refs.quote: Whether the defendant had sublet, assigned or otherwise parted with possession, of any part of the suit premises before the commencement of Act 38 of 1952 ?
Whether the defendant had sublet, assigned or otherwise parted with possession of any part of the suit premises after the commencement of Act 38 of 1952 ?
If so, was the same done with the prior consent in writing of the plaintiff ?

application_refs.quote: The respondent discharged the onus by leading evidence showing that the occupants were in exclusive possession of the apartments for valuable consideration.
In the absence of the best evidence of the grants, the Courts below properly inferred sub-lettings from the other materials on the record.
Where, as in this case, the hotel-keeper retains no control over the apart- ment, the occupier is in the position of a tenant.

The Courts below concurrently found that the sub-lettings after the commencement of the Act were made without obtaining the consent of the landlord in writing, and the sub-lettings before the commencement of the Act were made without obtaining the consent of the landlord either orally or in writing.
We are therefore satisfied that the respondent is entitled to evict the appellant on the ground of sub-letting of the rooms.

cases.law_scope: Delhi, India — civil lease/licence classification in a possession and accounts dispute; Indian Evidence Act, 1872 ss.91-92 and Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 s.16(2) are applied to the written agreement and the asserted sub-tenancy.
cases.target_stage: Supreme Court civil appeal arising out of S.L.P. (C) No. 5835/2001.
cases.substantive_issue: Whether the 15 May 1975 agency-cum-licence agreement was genuine and acted upon so that the appellant occupied as a licensee rather than as a lessee/sub-tenant.

issue_refs.quote: Before the High Court the parties agreed that the basic question which required consideration was whether relationship between the respondent and the appellant was that of licensor and licensee or it was that of lessor or lessee.
But the question is whether on the facts of the present case, the reasons given by the defendant-appellant in his evidence for claiming the agreement as sham document can be accepted.

application_refs.quote: As noticed by the High Court, the respondent-plaintiff No.1 had proved on record that the appellant-defendant had acted upon the agreement by himself, submitting the statements giving the account of tailoring and sale of materials as well as payment of commission on the basis of statements as per the terms of an agreement.
No explanation has been offered as to why cheques for amounts tallying with commissions, upto even paise were issued.

The High Court has also taken note of several other instances to conclude that the agreement was one of licence and not of lease. That being the position, the conclusions of the High Court are in order and do not warrant interference.
Since there is no consent of the landlord, something which is forbidden by law could not be pleaded. That being the position, the High Court was justified in rejecting the plea of sub-tenancy.

cases.law_scope: Delhi, India — Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, s.14(1)(e) and its Explanation concerning premises let for residential purposes but used incidentally for commercial or other purposes without landlord consent.
cases.target_stage: Supreme Court civil appeal (Civil Appeal No. 1993 of 1982) from the Delhi High Court judgment in S.A.O. No. 59 of 1979.
cases.substantive_issue: Whether the tenant's regular paying-guest/boarding-house use, with the landlord's knowledge and implied consent, took the premises outside the 'premises let for residential purposes' condition of s.14(1)(e) and its Explanation.

issue_refs.quote: Assuming that the bona fide requirement of the landlord is established, the landlord must still prove that the premises had been let for residential purposes.
The fundamental question in respect of residential premises is whether the landlord had consented to the user of the premises for any other purpose, albeit incidentally.

application_refs.quote: There is no substance in the contention that the landlord was unaware that the premises had been used for lodging foreign students.

In the present case, it is not disputed that the premises had been let for residential purposes, but it is also beyond doubt that to the knowledge of the landlord the premises have been regularly used by the tenant not only for her own residence but also for her foreign guests.
At no time did the landlord object to the user of the premises by the appellant for such purpose.

The continued user of the building ever since 1961 for the purpose of lodging paying guests shows that the respondent-landlord and her father have not only been aware of such user of the building, but have also impliedly consented to such user.
The evidence on record leaves no doubt that the premises have been regularly used by the appellant as a boarding house and not as a private 480 residence in the ordinary acceptation of the term.

allowed_spans.quote: The respondent is the daughter of the original landlord who had let out the premises to the appellant on 1.10.1961.

allowed_spans.quote: both the statutory authorities found that the premises which had been let out for residential purposes to the appellant had also been used incidentally for commercial purposes
allowed_spans.reason: Express concurrent finding of the two statutory fact-finding authorities.

allowed_spans.reason: Contrary High Court finding, preserved as a prior-stage finding rather than reconciled.

allowed_spans.quote: No documentary evidence has been brought on record to hold that the premises were ever used for boarding and lodging foreign students
allowed_spans.reason: Quoted High Court reasoning that supplies the opposing prior-court account.

allowed_spans.quote: The tenant contended that she had never parted with her exclusive possession of any part of the premises and the foreign students who were lodging were her paying guests and were not her tenants.
allowed_spans.reason: Tenant's earlier factual position on the character of the students' occupation.
